title: Synonymous Sentences
statement:
Each pair `[s, t]` in `synonyms` says that the words `s` and `t` mean the same thing. Synonymy works both ways and chains: if `a` is a synonym of `b` and `b` of `c`, then `a` and `c` are synonyms too, so the pairs split words into groups of interchangeable words.

`text` is a sentence of words separated by single spaces. Independently for every word of `text`, you may keep it or replace it with any word of its group; a word that appears in no pair must stay as it is. Return every sentence that can be produced this way (`text` itself included), each once, sorted in lexicographic order, where strings are compared character by character by character code.
constraints: No pair of words appears twice in synonyms
text has 1 to 10 words, separated by single spaces
Every word consists of English letters

examples.name: Example 1
input: I am happy today but was sad yesterday
expected: I am cheerful today but was sad yesterday
I am cheerful today but was sorrow yesterday
I am happy today but was sad yesterday
I am happy today but was sorrow yesterday
I am joy today but was sad yesterday
I am joy today but was sorrow yesterday

examples.name: Example 2
input: I am happy today but was sad yesterday
expected: I am happy today but was sad yesterday
I am joy today but was sad yesterday

tests.name: Test 9
input: one two three four five six

notes:
## Intuition

Because synonymy chains, the pairs are edges of a graph and the interchangeable words are its connected components. Union-find builds those groups directly: each pair merges two sets. After that every word of `text` has a fixed list of options (its group, or just itself), and the answer is every combination of options, which backtracking lists one word at a time. Sorting each group first makes the sentences come out already in order: letters all come after the space character, so comparing sentences character by character agrees with comparing them word by word. (The brute force instead keeps swapping single words for direct synonyms until no new sentence appears, then sorts.)

## Approach

1. Give every word in a pair its own set in `parent`, then `find` both words of each pair and link one root to the other.
2. Collect `groups`: each root maps to the list of words in its set. Sort each list.
3. Split `text` into `words`. `build(index)` chooses a word for position `index`: every word of its group if the word is in `parent`, otherwise the word itself.
4. For each option, push it on `current`, build the rest, and pop it again.
5. When `index` reaches the end, join `current` with spaces into `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

The pairs give two groups: `{happy, joy, cheerful}` and `{sad, sorrow}`, sorted as `[cheerful, happy, joy]` and `[sad, sorrow]`. `build` keeps `I` and `am`, tries `cheerful` first, keeps `today but was`, then tries `sad` and `sorrow`, producing `I am cheerful today but was sad yesterday` and `... sorrow yesterday`. Then `happy` and `joy` give two sentences each: six sentences, already sorted.

## Complexity

- Time: O(P α(P) + R · L), where P is the number of pairs, R the number of sentences and L the length of a sentence: union-find is nearly linear and each sentence is built once.
- Space: O(R · L) for the answer, plus O(P) for the groups.

## Pitfalls

- Treating only direct pairs as synonyms: `happy` and `cheerful` are linked through `joy`.
- Forgetting that a word keeps its own spelling as one option: `text` itself must be in the answer.
- Sorting the words of a group is enough here only because spaces sort before letters; sorting the final list is the safe fallback.
- Looking up `groups.get(word)` instead of `groups.get(find(word))`: groups are stored under their root.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `parent` | union-find parent of each synonym word |
| `find` | returns a word's root, halving paths on the way |
| `groups` | root to the sorted list of words in its group |
| `words` | the words of `text` |
| `current` | the words chosen so far for the sentence being built |
| `options` | the words that may stand at the current position |
| `result` | every sentence, in sorted order |
